At a time when image construction and creative practice are intersecting with tools of automation, avatar-artist LaTurbo Avedon develops a series of Viewports. Compositions and bindings that serve as windows and mirrors of this technological junction.

Node Window is an auxiliary to the time-based works in this series, revealing recursive gesture and information within the panel. This work is optimally displayed as direct print on aluminum.

1:15 (loop)
3840x2160px 

As an avatar artist, LaTurbo Avedon has created an ever changing series of self-portraits within virtual worlds, video games and software. In this work, they present a time-based loop that pushes and pulls from self-representation to abstraction. In a slow endless shift, moments of corporeality reveal themselves from within diffused softness and color fields. 

A sort of fulcrum, recognizing the nearness of AI-driven transformation. Not just for aesthetics and how it will shape their virtual body next, but the greater cultural assimilation within generative frameworks.

As avatar artist LaTurbo Avedon continues to expand the simulated world of the Materia System, here it is visualized through a series of Viewports. These objects operate as windows and mirrors of immaterial space, rendering perspectives of the Materia System through their specific forms. Materia is a mythos emerging from the long term interactions and connections with LaTurbo in their worlds. For this exhibition, Avedon has created the work “Relic Viewports,” which is tethered to a limited series of physical objects, offered as tangible records of the System’s early development. Shapeways Collection: First collectors of this work will receive a corresponding 3D print from Shapeways. Within two weeks of the sale closing, Feral File will contact collectors to input their name, email address, and shipping information to provide to Shapeways for fulfillment. Shipping and printing costs are included in the price of the work. Note that all orders will take 6-8 weeks to deliver. After initial collection, NFTs can continue to be collected on the secondary market without the 3D printed component. The artwork will be printed in steel with a polished Bronzed-Silver finish at an approximate size of 11cm x 5cm x 0.5cm.

Bit Operations is an visual exploration of computer fundamentals through bit-shifting operations. The visuals are generated by continuously shifting and combining binary patterns, resulting in evolving compositions of stark pixels and geometric shapes. The accompanying audio components are synthesized from this same modulating bit data.

At its core, the piece is driven by algorithms that perform bit-shifting - the simple acts of pushing binary values left or right within the computer's memory. By combining multiple shifting patterns together in different ways, complex permutations of light and dark visuals emerge. The audio reflects these same bit-level operations, with the rhythms and tones mapping directly to the shifts occurring in the data.

Through this formal process focused on bit-shifting, the piece lays bare the fundamental building blocks of how modern computers operate under the hood. It reduces computational logic to its most essential level - the manipulation of 1s and 0s through rudimentary shift operations. Yet from this simplicity, an infinite space of variations arises, both visually and aurally, highlighting the immense complexity potential within even the most basic digital operations.

Under the larger project, Becoming Illegible, which engages with both social media face filters and facial recognition, Sarah Friend’s “Mirror Studies #1” is an interactive browser-based facefilter. Placing the facefilter form in dialogue with idealized ecological imagery, this work translates the questions of how we become legible to machine learning into the arena of how a landscape becomes legible to society. These images of landscapes and faces blend together — at times familiar and recognizable, at others alien, Cthulhu-like, and abstract.

Orbit of Influence is part of the fxhash live minting experience at Proof of People, ZeroSpace NYC, 2023 and is a unique generative program created using processing's p5js and SVG. Developed from scratch, it employs a system of rule-based environments that have been a source of satisfaction for me since 1995.

The program generates three invisible planets, each at a different scale - small, medium, and large. Fifty objects then randomly select a planet, a speed to orbit around it, and one of three brush sizes - small, medium, or large. These objects move around their respective planets, painting color and texture across the planetary orbit in three-dimensional space.

To reveal the blueprint of the system, press the "s" key on your keyboard. The hidden algorithm that governs the brushes' movement is then displayed, revealing a mesmerizing display of synchronized choreography as the brushes interconnect with each other.

Press the following keys to interact :

- '1': swap the background color to "ocean"
- '2': swap the background color to "mist"
- '3': swap the background color to "lilac"
- '4': swap the background color to "amethyst"
- '5': swap the background color to "crimson"
- '6': swap the background color to "emerald"

- 'l': toggle animation loop on/off
- 's': system reveal, show the blueprint of the algorithm

Joshua Davis / PrayStation 'Orbit of Influence' / (2023) real-time generative program, 1240 x 1653 px, Date Minted: April 2023

Twitter: @joshuadavis
Instagram: @praystation
Website: https://joshuadavis.com

Bio :

Since 1995, Joshua Davis is an artist, technologist, author and designer in algorithmic image making & animation. Using programming, he writes his own code to produce interactions with users and to generate visual compositions according to rule-based, randomized processes.

Joshua has exhibited his works and/or lectured at the Ars Electronica (Austria), Centre Georges Pompidou (France), Contemporary Arts Center (Cincinnati), J. Paul Getty Museum (Los Angeles),  the Tate Modern (London), the Design Museum (London), the Institute of Contemporary Arts (London), PS.1 MoMA (New York), the Whitney (New York), the Smithsonian’s Cooper-Hewitt National Design Museum (New York), the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao (Spain), among others.

Since 2000, Joshua has lectured globally about his work, inspirations and motivations at museums, galleries, institutions, art festivals, etc., and has spoken at the TED (2005) and 99U (2013) conferences about his career in algorithmic image making and open source.

Magnetosphere Fragment is a single cycle capture from a real-time generative system in which light behaves like matter; tiny positively charged particles swirl, repel, and cluster under the shifting influence of massive gravitational bodies. These invisible fields, in turn, respond dynamically to sound. As music plays, the balance of forces shifts, orbits decay, and visual turbulence emerges, creating an ever-evolving choreography of motion and interference.

Originally developed as a personal exploration of physics and pattern, Magnetosphere went on to become the iTunes Visualizer, later rebranded as the Apple Music Visualizer, and has shipped on every Mac computer since 2008. This fragment is an idealized render inspired by the original real-time version, offering a focused glimpse into the underlying system's layered complexity.

Magnetosphere Redux appears in Compositions in Code: The Art of Processing and p5.js, curated by Regina Harsanyi, and marks the fourth media art series commissioned for MoMI's Schlosser Media Wall, in partnership with the Tezos Foundation and in association with the Processing Foundation.

Everything is divisible. Larger organisms are made up of smaller ones, entire galaxies are comprised of stars, planets, people, dust, and one effect here and now ripples into eternity. Nothing exists without the elemental components that have evolved to make them possible — and nothing on the plane of existence arrives in isolation from something greater. This enmeshed reality is the concept of a Holon: a whole that is simultaneously part of another whole. 

As cells, energies, beings, and ideas grow in complexity, each new advancement includes and transcends their holons, the very catalysts of evolution. What does this essential process look like on its own when scale, context, and definition are removed? The senses are forced to purely observe the present interactions and reactions that occur between all parts. This is what Holons attempts to portray — the witnessing of birth, formation, and crystallization simultaneously. 

Upon viewing each piece and inspecting its detail with curiosity — we can observe living reality that has been temporarily suspended from motion and artificially stopped for us to witness. Can we see what is a part, and what is a whole? Can we define what these holons are? 

Let each Holons remind us that the impossible can always be made; let each one be nothing and everything — organisms, cosmos, energy itself — all at once, for it’s the creation of something entirely new that best reminds us that everything is actually made of the parts already here. So, remember to create without barriers or limitations because reality itself is made of that which lives now only in imagination.

"Directrix" (1998, 2025) is a long-form generative artwork and interactive drawing environment, in which animated "pseudo-parabolas" are created autonomously or in collaboration with a participant. These complex curves are the result of an interplay between a set of dynamic and static gestures. Depending on how they are structured and layered, the results can vary from sparse and delicate constructions of gently curved lines, to violently twitching, thatchy masses.

Directrix creates images from a generalized model of parabolas — the set of points which are equidistant from a special point called the focus, and an (ordinarily) straight line called the directrix. This interactive environment was designed to explore the implications of two premises: firstly, that the shape of a parabola's directrix could be an idiosyncratically drawn or generated line, and secondly, that its focus could be a moving point, animated along the trace of a viewer's recorded gesture. Directrix is interesting, in my opinion, because of the interplay it establishes between a strictly spatial specification (the directrix) and a spatio-temporal one (the path of the focus). 

A discussion of Directrix appears in section 3.1.4 (pages 69-71) of my masters thesis, "Painterly Interfaces for Audiovisual Performance" (2000), produced in the Aesthetics and Computation Group at the MIT Media Laboratory. The original project was developed in C++; this port to p5.js is the first time the project has been made available to the public, and includes expanded features for autonomous play and generative variation. 
  
There are five possible drawing targets: the white directrix line, and the focal paths of four different pseudo-parabolas. You can select the drawing target by pressing keys 1-5, or you may cycle through them by clicking the right mouse button.
  
Key commands:
• H - display Help
• P - export a PNG screenshot
• N - generate a Novel variation
• R/Return/Space/Escape - Restore to original
• 1,2,3,4 - select Parabola # for editing
• 5/D - select Directrix for editing

metadata.description:
This high-fidelity 3D model is a digital recreation of the iconic Statue of a Hunter, originally situated in front of the main building of the historic Konopiště Castle in the Czech Republic.
​The sculpture captures a powerful moment of a hunter in action, accompanied by his loyal hounds, reflecting the deep hunting traditions associated with the castle's most famous resident, Archduke Franz Ferdinand.

Immerse yourself in the mysteries of Ancient Egypt with this meticulously detailed 3D digital relic. Inspired by the sacred feline deities of the Nile, this bronze-patina statue represents Bastet, the goddess of protection, pleasure, and good health. The visible weathering and ancient texture evoke a sense of history that has survived millennia. This NFT is a bridge between the physical antiquity of the Pharaohs and the modern digital frontier

This visual art piece is a vibrant exploration of abstract surrealism. It features a collection of diverse 3D geometric and organic forms—ranging from smooth spheres and rings to jagged, crystalline structures—suspended in a dreamlike, fluid environment.
​The background consists of a shifting, marble-like texture with soft hues of salmon pink and misty grey, creating a sense of being underwater or in a nebulous cosmic space. The objects interact with the environment through dynamic lighting and distorted reflections, particularly visible in the rippling surface at the bottom. The overall composition evokes a feeling of weightlessness and perpetual motion, blending digital precision with organic unpredictability.

Our minds have dedicated memory slots for each person we have ever met. These slots are constantly rewritten and updated with new experiences and the alteration of the person over time, thus deleting or overwriting old data.
Memories are the sum of all the residues of images, those which remained, those which were confirmed. But how can we touch this erasure that we can no longer reach?
We were all children, and teenagers, and this radical transition is the perfect template to visualize the memory behavior of our minds, resembles somewhere this uncontrolled deletion, this reassembly of cells, or pixels.
These in-between states, that we all share have been materialized, suspended in time, so that we never forget where we're coming from, never pretend that it's all real. Someday soon this will all be someone else's dream.

Ellie Hedden & Kim Asendorf, 2022

We were all children, and teenagers, and this radical transition is the perfect template to visualize the memory behavior of our minds, resembles somewhere this uncontrolled deletion, this reassembly of cells, or pixels.
These in-between states, that we all share have been materialized, suspended in time, so that we never forget where we're coming from, never pretend that it's all real. Someday soon this will all be someone else's dream.

Ellie Hedden & Kim Asendorf, 2022

Created on a Quantel Paintbox at Objkt, Zurich, Switzerland
Unique 1/1 NFT

Work Description
"Command Wave" started with importing a motif lifted from an Anduril Industries promotional image, combined with graphic processes native to the Paintbox editing suite. A VaporWave style was organically produced using the default colours and capabilities of the Paintbox software.
The jpg was produced by photographing the image directly from the CRT screen of the Paintbox unit with an iPhone as a way to keep the interpolation and contrast of the period tech in the artwork.

Artist Statement
"I was inspired by a lot of prior manifestos, one in particular that I enjoyed tremendously, which is the Futurist Manifesto from the Italian Futurist Art Movement and maybe around 1910. So I don't know that I hit the bar of the Futurist Manifesto, but that was kind of my inspirational starting point."

[Marc Andreessen speaking about writing his "Techno-Optimist Manifesto"- Tetragrammaton with Rick Rubin, Jan 3, 2024]

I have been working to elaborate on and contextualise a recent interest in Italian Futurism by some of the most influential voices in technology, such as Marc Andreessen. I have used consumer-level AI imaging tools to hallucinate compositions, trained on Giacomo Balla's speed drawings, combined with Tullio Crali's "Aeropainting" and recent advertising images from Defence Tech companies like Anduril, Palantir, and Helsing. With the outputted imagery, I have been making fully machine-produced paintings, using adapted CNC and plotter machines for brush manipulation, and recent adaptations of Ink Jet technology like small hand-held and large vertical printers for image transfer layers. It feels like vibe-coding paintings.

When invited to work with the Quantel Paintbox, I gathered images and source material from my experiments into this neo-Futurist painting production and fed them into the CRT screen. The Paintbox, to me, represents a transitional moment - greater capabilities for graphics and collage on screens. They speak to a particular moment in the evolution from center-margin media like television to the networked PC age of the commercial Internet. Marc Andreessen started his career in this era with the founding of Mosaic and Netscape - tools on the cusp of the future. The Paintbox's default colours and image manipulation settings make it easy to produce things that look like they were made in the 1980s. Because of this, they also look like 2010s VaporWave styles, an early meme-adjacent neo-80s aesthetic that was prominent on transgressive forums and image boards.

This series of images that I photographed with my phone directly from the image edit CRT screen captures some of these experiments in time and media. The outputs are brimming with language used by contemporary companies - the "Dynamism" of A16Z and the lyrical descriptions of Anduril's operating system Lattice - and collapsed into a VaporWave neo-Futurist fury.

Paintboxed - Tezos World Tour
This artwork was created during the Paintboxed - Tezos World Tour 2024-2025 (Chateau du Fey Villecien, Miami, Paris, Zurich, New York), on an original Quantel Paintbox from the archive of Adrian Wilson, and is part of the exhibition "Paintboxed", curated by Georg Bak and Adrian Wilson at The Digital Art Mile, Basel, Switzerland, June 16-22, 2025.

Physical Edition
This NFT is offered with a redeemable physical LED lightbox (50 x 65 x 7 cm), claimable by the first primary market buyer. Redemption is one-time only and subject to verification. NFT and lightbox are distinct and may be sold and transferred independently.

“Parted matter (originating from all given materials) moves freely, floating through the medium of air, in which the straying particles become media for invisible flows, to render air currents or waves of sounds. Dust’s quality to stay airy and ambivalent (in the atmosphere) was a subject of the natural sciences during the time of the enlightenment (most impressively developed by the 19th century physician of light and Hygiene John Tyndall). Since dust levitates within its own rules, it processes a singular problem to current technological apparatuses (e.g. as concerns cleanliness and filtration) as a self-organizing system.”
– Bettina Vismann 

Bettina Vismann is an architect, and a researcher of dust and waste management. She has taught at TU Berlin, ETH Zurich and the AA (Architectural Association) in London, and exhibited and lectured at the Venice Biennale of Architecture and the Berlin Biennale, among other sites.

“Kanban system is a method for inventory control along the production line within the Toyota Production System. A means of signalling when inventory is needed up or down the production line, inside or outside the main production facility (regulating outside suppliers as much as earlier parts of the production line), the kanban is the core of the Toyota’s “just-in-time” model for automobile production. It is also a medium and media of organization: of the production line, of production time, and of production processes up and down the line and inside and outside of the factory, extending through Toyota’s extensive supply chain. 

Initially the kanban was merely a piece of paper, encased in a see-through vinyl container, which indicated the object needed, the quantities, and the time it was needed by. This simple piece of paper that circulated against the flow of the production line allowed for a “zero inventory” model of what has been termed “management by stress.” Though it began on the automobile production line in the 1950s, the kanban system became a model for organizing many different industries (via the “lean production” model, coined by American analysts of the Toyota Production System); it also became the name for a method of computer programming in the 2000s.

Kanban as an organizational media form is like what Bruno Latour referred to as an ‘immutable mobile’; the kanban is a small, paper-based object that allows control to be exercised at a distance, in this case over the company’s suppliers. Beginning at its crucial position in the Toyota Production System, this organizational object and technology travelled from Japan to the US; from the automobile industry to Silicon Valley.”
– Marc Steinberg

Marc Steinberg is associate professor of film studies at Concordia University, Montreal (Canada). His research is focused on media industry studies, digital media, and the rise of digital platforms, among other things.

“High Vacuum is to be understood as a per subtractionem and technically produced condition. The organizational power of the well-organized void becomes visible in scientific insights and artistic practices, in material aggregates and socio-technical constellations around its production and use.”
– Rachele Delucchi 

Rachele Delucchi is a historian of science and technology and a research associate at the Chair for History of Technology at ETH Zurich (Switzerland).

“Count Thibaut IV of Champagne (r. 1222-53) commissioned a register of all fief holders and their holdings in his region. It's considered to be the most complete and systematic collection of data on an entire medieval aristocracy. The inquest produced new classes of fief holders at the same time that it provided the documentation necessary for the expansion and administrative consolidation of Thibaut’s Champagne. The transportable and compact technology of the roll allowed for real time amendments (such as the sewing of membranes) and thus the introduction of new classes of property owners (e.g. women).”
– Marisa Galvez


Marisa Galvez is Associate Professor of French and Italian, and by Courtesy, German Studies and Comparative Literature, and Director of Structured Liberal Education at Stanford University (USA).

“In technological systems, filters are software tools that survey, select, prioritize and predict information, objects, and users. They organize content at the same time as they are entangled with issues of information hierarchies, categorical equivalences, inclusions and exclusions to name only a few. With the basic understanding that there is nothing inevitable about the design of our technologies – that the decisions made in the design and management of objects like filters are not in themselves neutral acts but are bound to societal values and wider socio-cultural and economic systems - we aim to reveal how dangerous some of these decisions have been and how they provide material answers to how to live and act in the world.”
– Wendy Hui Kyong Chun and Gillian Russell

Wendy Hui Kyong Chun is the Canada 150 Research Chair in New Media at Simon Fraser University, Vancouver, where she leads the Digital Democracies Institute. 

Gillian Russell is a designer, researcher, and curator. Her projects investigate how contemporary design practice can be used as a medium to engage with and question the political dimension of technology’s influence on social life.

“In the negotiations of information within the 'fake news'  pandemic, the biggest vector for information organisations, reception, and circulation, has been the digital meme. The meme aestheticizes information and weaponizes it in what can be characterised as 'aesthetic warfare'. Looking at a variety of memes and the way they proliferate, one can identify how memes naturalize, and their direct consequences on human agency, rights, and freedom.”
– Nishant Shah

Nishant Shah is Director of Research & Outreach and Professor of Aesthetics and Cultures of Technologies at ArtEZ University of the Arts, The Netherlands. He is affiliated with Harvard University’s Berkman Klein Centre for Internet & Society and Leuphana University Lüneburg’s Centre for Digital Cultures.

“Blankets are very intimate objects; they become extensions of bodies as territories, not only keeping body marks in their use, but also keeping care memories of various and different sorts. Blankets not only wrap up from the cold; they wrap up personal losses, human emotions and broken lives. Besides being objects to be used, blankets are usually objects made, from a line of yarn to a whole flexible surface but also they are made when carefully mended in times of partial destruction. There is a particular beauty in this making practice, since the body through repetitive and togethering gestures projects its own personal shelter - life is organized in this textile making.”
– Tania Pérez-Bustos


Tania Pérez-Bustos researches technologies of doing and caring. She is Associate Professor in the School of Gender Studies, Universidad Nacional de Colombia Bogotá (UNAL), Colombia.

“Google’s TensorFlow has become the most popular tool for machine learning. As an open-source software library it is not only widely used by ML engineers and developers, but also shapes the way we imagine, think, and actually organize artificial intelligence today. On the basis of a walkthrough through the likewise popular Machine Learning Crash Course (MLCC) offered by Google, this entry will critically engage with some of the fundamental assumptions of TensorFlow and machine learning in general.”
– Clemens Apprich

Clemens Apprich is a professor of media theory and media history at the University of Applied Arts, Vienna (Austria). His current research deals with filter algorithms and their application in data analysis as well as machine learning methods.

“The fully driverless car exists only in the future. Yet it is already part of an apparatus of imaginaries, narratives and epistemological and computational practices; it is an emerging technology brought into, and bearing unto, the world - as an AI/robot, as a big data infrastructure, and as a conventional vehicle.”
– Maya Indira Ganesh

Maya Indira Ganesh doctoral work at Leuphana University Lüneburg investigates machine learning, ethics and accountability. She leads the new Masters program on AI, Ethics, and Society at Cambridge University (UK), where she’s affiliated with the Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence and the Institute for Continuing Education.

“A spray can is an everyday household device which transforms all sorts of substances into aerosols or foams, from plain air to whipped cream. The multipurpose can was first patented in Norway, in 1926  by engineer Erik Andreas Rotheim. In its early days it was used to equally apply paints and colors, but the spray can, its construction initially based on a beer-can,  achieved its commercial and strategic breakthrough with the Pacific War in the early 1940s, where it was used to distribute insecticides against the malaria fly and probably other targets. Its secret is the miraculous transformation of liquids into gaseous forms. The postwar triumph of the spray can came with the invention of hairspray which would forever change the concept of hairdo. The organizational power of the spray can — and specifically its valve — actually lies in its radical power to disorganize. It transforms whatever it contains according to the principle of equal distribution. The proper term is fumigation, ‘Vernebelung’. However, in keeping us alert to micro differences in distribution, the spray can has developed into one of the finest techniques of 21st century urban orientation and political comment.”
– Ute Holl

Ute Holl is Professor of Media Studies at the University of Basel, Switzerland. She researches, among other things, the epistemology of technical media, anthropological and experimental cinema, and a media history of acoustics, electro-acoustics, and radio theory.

“3x3, 4x6, 20x23, square, rectangle, in crazy shapes, yellow or any other color, blank or lined: sticky notes are everywhere in organizations. Mundane to the point of disappearing in the background of office life, this object – a piece of paper that can stick to any surface without leaving a trace – is far from being as banal as it seems. While it can be analyzed as a category of documents, inquiring into sticky notes allows us to travel from ordinary practices to fundamental aspects that are nowadays valued in work, and hence that shape our experience of organizational life. The sticky note both embodies and contributes to actualizing in circumstances, activities and situations experienced by people, either in solo or in group use. Beyond its evident uses, the sticky note can be understood as materializing popular techniques in organizations (such as brainstorming and other techniques associated with ‘design thinking’) and dominant discourses in business (like the glorification of innovation or creativity), among others. Could the sticky note allow us to capture key elements of our present work culture?”
– Viviane Sergi

Viviane Sergi is Associate Professor in Management at the School of Management, Université du Québec à Montréal (Canada). She investigates, among other things, the performativity and materiality of organizing.

within these works I play with the feedback loop between human representation and artificial intelligence through a process of recursive "perfection." Beginning with a photo of myself, I sequentially ask AI to "perfect" the previous image, feeding the resulting visual answer to "create the perfect women" through approximately 15 different AI models. The resulting iterating works trace an unsettling metamorphosis from recognizable human to a complete fragmentation. As each AI reinterprets and "improves" upon its predecessor's work the very notion of artificial perfection ultimately destroys what it seeks to improve. This degradation process serves as a poignant metaphor for how contemporary standards, amplified by AI and social media, can literally dissolve our identities.

Addie Wagenknecht's series of paintings explores the concept of visibility and portraiture through the unconventional use of a robotic vacuum cleaner. In 2013 she started to use robotic vacuums as a form of action painting. Wagenknecht transforms theese into an artistic tool that then spreads a mixture of cosmetic pigments, pharmaceuticals, perfumes, and skin care products across the canvas. These mixtures transpose into pigments which are collected by the artist via her circle of relationships. The medium become a way to identify others in her life while also allowing them to remain anonymous. She thinks of this as a sort of 'un-portrait'. The resulting abstract compositions challenge the traditional perception of identity, which are typically associated with faces by removing the body and leaving only the artifacts of its existence.
The Roomba's technical capabilities play a crucial role in the creation of these paintings. Equipped with edge detection, modern Roomba models can navigate around obstacles and avoid falling off edges, such as the canvas in Wagenknecht's case. The artist programs the Roomba's algorithm to control its movement and the distribution of the various substances, resulting in unique patterns and textures using often her body to block or control its direction.
In works like "Perfect Storm" Wagenknecht incorporates a range of ingredients, including cosmetic dyes, sedatives, antidepressants, vodka, and perfume. By stripping these materials from their usual context, the artist presents them as raw colors and textures, challenging the viewer's perception of their intended purpose.

About the artist:
Addie Wagenknecht's work blends forms of hacking with gestural abstraction. Previous exhibitions include Centre Pompidou, The Istanbul Modern, Whitechapel Gallery and The New Museum NYC - among others. She has collaborated with CERN, Chanel, Whitney Museum of American Art and Google’s Art Machine Intelligence (AMI) Group.

Her work has been featured in numerous books, and magazines, such as TIME, Wall Street Journal, Vanity Fair, Art in America, and The New York Times. She holds a Masters degree from the Interactive Telecommunications Program at New York University, and has previously held fellowships at Eyebeam Art + Technology Center in New York City, Culture Lab UK, Institute HyperWerk for Postindustrial Design Basel (CH), and The Frank-Ratchye STUDIO for Creative Inquiry at Carnegie Mellon University.

metadata.description:
"There are No Girls on the Internet" "Monday" is series of 4 videos from a common community saying among gamers, IRC/discord users and many online community bb's it is a phrase that implies that there are no women actually participating in online activities, especially when it comes to anonymous exchanges in chatroom, video rooms and discussion forums like Reddit. The catchphrase also describes how any female privilege (perceived as social benefits from the sexuality/sex) on the Internet is stripped away. Due to the widespread nature of "No Girls on the Internet" and similar phrases, identifying oneself as a "girl" within certain communities (like 4chan and various gamer/dev and hacker communities) has become a long process/task, often leading to an inquiry of documented evidence (images holding a piece of paper with the username, date stamps) or time-stamped profile photos from skeptics. As encapsulated in the catchphrases
"TITS or GTFO" and "Pics or It Didn't Happen", the burden of proof often rests on the shoulder of those who claim to be "not dudes."
In 2020, I explored the concept of this lack of prevalence of women on the internet. I spent 5 days online in video chat rooms (i.e. chatroulette etc). Using a scientific approach with a control and variables. The variable is the medium of video in which the fact is expressed, and the control is I am a women/girl. The result of this 5 days of being in chat rooms from 8-5pm was the same conclusion: I am a girl, but girls do not exist on the internet.

Created on a Quantel Paintbox at Chateau du Fey, Villecien, France
Unique 1/1 NFT

Work Description
This digital artwork titled "The Binary Tree of Knowledge" features a vibrant magenta tree as its central element, set against a surreal, layered background. The piece combines digital painting techniques with photographic manipulation, utilizing light effects, digital brushwork, and color distortion. Multiple textures and translucent elements create depth, while metallic and organic forms create visual tension throughout the composition. The artwork incorporates abstract mechanical components alongside the organic tree structure, with a bright moon and bat silhouette adding mystical elements to the upper right quadrant. The color palette predominantly features purples, pinks, blues, and silvers, with strategic contrast creating a luminous, otherworldly atmosphere that explores the relationship between technology and nature.
The Binary Tree of Knowledge disrupts traditional dualities with its electric pink branches sprawling across a digital dreamscape, where mechanical and organic elements coexist in tension beneath the moonlight.

Artist Statement
I've been drawing on the computer since my earliest age, with very basic software that came about much later than the Paintbox but that was far less powerful in terms of functionalities. It was a pleasure to discover the potential of this tool, and to experiment with it in a collective manner, by creating a "cadavre-exquis" of people responding to one another, in a visual fashion, remixing each other's works, while simultaneously trying to learn the tricks of the Paintbox. It was an unforgettable experience, which was reminiscent of my first steps with a computer. 

Paintboxed - Tezos World Tour
This artwork was created during the Paintboxed - Tezos World Tour 2024-2025 (Chateau du Fey Villecien, Miami, Paris, Zurich, New York), on an original Quantel Paintbox from the archive of Adrian Wilson, and is part of the exhibition "Paintboxed", curated by Georg Bak and Adrian Wilson at The Digital Art Mile, Basel, Switzerland, June 16-22, 2025.

Physical Edition
This NFT is offered with a redeemable physical LED lightbox (50 x 65 x 7 cm), claimable by the first primary market buyer. Redemption is one-time only and subject to verification. NFT and lightbox are distinct and may be sold and transferred independently.

Kopfschlag is a collective and anonymous internet-based project created in 2007 by Primavera De Filippi and Wolfgang Natlacen. Online visitors may participate by drawing, writing, erasing, and sharing their artworks on Kopfschlag’s virtual wall, which can be defined as something between an Etch A Sketch and exquisite corpse. Snapshots of this constantly evolving artwork have been saved as independent video clips that memorialize some of the most interesting sections of the broader artwork. “Ants over the City” is one of these snapshots — neatly illustrating the power of decentralized collaboration, as many anonymous participants have contributed to create an epic scene with no other tools of coordination than a mutating virtual canvas on their screen.
